Auberive
oh-buh-REEV
n. (a Cistercian abbey in the Haute-Marne, founded 1135 as a daughter of Clairvaux; its buildings served as a prison in the nineteenth century)
From Latin alba ripa, the white bank, through Old French; named for the pale bank of the Aube valley.

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

Auberive was founded in 1135 in the upper Aube valley of Champagne, a daughter of Clairvaux, and rebuilt in the eighteenth century. Sold at the Revolution, its ranges were converted in the nineteenth century into a house of detention — first for political prisoners, later a women's prison and reformatory — and the cloister that had been built for monks held inmates for decades. The reversal is worth more than irony, because the care of prisoners is a duty Scripture lays on the church in the plainest terms. “I was in prison, and ye came unto me” (Mat 25:36) sets Christ himself in the cell; “Remember them that are in bonds, as bound with them; and them which suffer adversity, as being yourselves also in the body” (Heb 13:3) asks for identification and not merely charity; and the messianic commission includes release: “he hath sent me to bind up the brokenhearted, to proclaim liberty to the captives, and the opening of the prison to them that are bound” (Isa 61:1). An abbey that became a prison was given, late and unintentionally, a mission field at its own address.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines prison as a public building for the confinement of debtors and criminals; captive as a prisoner taken by force or stratagem; and bonds as chains, fetters, that which confines or restrains.

expand to see more

PRISON, n. A public building for the confinement or safe custody of debtors and criminals committed by process of law; a jail.

CAPTIVE, n. A prisoner taken by force or stratagem in war, by an enemy; also, one who is charmed or subdued.

BOND, n. Any thing that binds, as a cord, a chain, a rope; a band; in the plural, chains; imprisonment; captivity.

DETENTION, n. The act of detaining; a keeping back; a withholding; confinement; restraint.

LIBERTY, n. Freedom from restraint, in a general sense; natural liberty, civil liberty, political liberty, spiritual liberty.

Key Scripture

Mat 25:36 — "Naked, and ye clothed me: I was sick, and ye visited me: I was in prison, and ye came unto me."

Heb 13:3 — "Remember them that are in bonds, as bound with them; and them which suffer adversity, as being yourselves also in the body."

Isa 61:1 — "The Spirit of the Lord GOD is upon me; because the LORD hath anointed me to preach good tidings unto the meek; he hath sent me to bind up the brokenhearted, to proclaim liberty to the captives, and the opening of the prison to them that are bound;"

Luk 4:18 — "The Spirit of the Lord is upon me, because he hath anointed me to preach the gospel to the poor; he hath sent me to heal the brokenhearted, to preach deliverance to the captives, and recovering of sight to the blind, to set at liberty them that are bruised,"

Modern Corruption

A Clairvaux daughter of 1135 whose cloister became a nineteenth-century prison: a mission field delivered, late and unintentionally, to its own address.

expand to see more

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is prison visiting as an unavoidable Christian duty. “Remember them that are in bonds, as bound with them” (Heb 13:3) is not satisfied by sympathy at a distance, and the great majority of congregations do nothing about it at all.

The second thing to notice is the scope of the messianic commission, which includes the cell by name: “to preach deliverance to the captives, and recovering of sight to the blind, to set at liberty them that are bruised” (Luk 4:18). Christ read that passage in a synagogue and said it was fulfilled in him. A church that reads it as metaphor only has cut out half of what he claimed.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Latin alba ripa, white bank; Hebrew shebi (H7628), captivity; Hebrew asir (H616), a prisoner; Greek desmos (G1199), a bond; Greek aphesis (G859), release.

expand to see more

Latin alba ripa — the white bank; the abbey named for the pale valley side.

Hebrew asir (H616) — a prisoner, one bound; the Psalter's word for those God hears.

Hebrew shebi (H7628) — captivity; “to proclaim liberty to the captives” (Isa 61:1).

Greek desmos (G1199) — a bond, fetter; “Remember them that are in bonds” (Heb 13:3).

Greek aphesis (G859) — release, remission; “to preach deliverance to the captives” (Luk 4:18).

Usage

"“I was in prison, and ye came unto me” (Mat 25:36) — Christ identified with the prisoner."

"“as being yourselves also in the body” (Heb 13:3) — identification, not distant pity."

"“the opening of the prison to them that are bound” (Isa 61:1) — part of the commission Christ claimed."
